# Editing Grammar

Editing AI-generated clips follows the same principles as editing any footage — because the problems you're solving (temporal logic, spatial coherence, rhythm, emotional momentum) are the same. What's different is that each clip arrives with its own independent colour grade, its own motion signature, and potential frame-level artifacts at its head and tail.

---

## Assembly order

1. **Rough cut** — lay clips in story order, evaluate spatial and temporal logic before any colour or audio work
2. **Trim heads and tails** — remove artifact frames at clip boundaries
3. **Apply cut-hide technique** at joins
4. **Colour match** across clips
5. **Add J/L-cuts** for audio continuity
6. **Sound design and scoring**
7. **Final review** for eyeline logic, screen direction, pacing

Never colour before cutting. Never score before pacing is locked. The order matters.

---

## Trimming heads and tails

AI-generated clips — particularly I2V (image-to-video) and clips generated by chaining — frequently carry artifact frames at the beginning and end: a slightly distorted frame as the model initialises from the reference image, or a subtle reverse-motion artifact at the tail as the model resolves the clip.

**Trim approximately 4 frames (~0.17 seconds at 24fps) from the head and tail of every AI clip before assembly.** [PRACTITIONER — reported as a consistent working practice; check your specific model's output]

4-frame cross-dissolves between adjacent AI clips also help — they soften seams that would be visible as hard cuts.

---

## Cut-hide technique

The cut-hide technique places the edit point where foreground motion masks the seam. A character turning, a hand crossing frame, a door passing the camera — any moving element that briefly fills enough of the frame to disguise the cut point.

This technique exists in live-action editing (matching on the swish of a coat) and is equally useful in AI assembly, where adjacent clips may have different colour or slightly different spatial geometry.

**How to design for it:** when writing prompts, specify exit and entry motion that is designed for a cut-hide. If clip A ends with A turning toward the door, prompt clip B (the next angle) to begin with A completing that turn — and place the cut at the peak of the motion.

---

## J-cuts and L-cuts

These are post-production editorial techniques, not generated in the clips themselves.

**J-cut:** the audio from the incoming shot is heard while the outgoing shot's image is still on screen. The audience hears the next scene before they see it. Creates anticipation.

**L-cut:** the audio from the outgoing shot continues while the incoming shot's image is already on screen. Creates continuity and immersion.

Both are applied in the NLE (DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, etc.) by separating the audio and video tracks of adjacent clips and trimming each independently. No generator produces these natively as of mid-2026.

---

## Colour matching

Each clip grades independently because each is generated independently. On a timeline, unmatched clips read as if the scene jumped between three different films.

**Fastest workflow: DaVinci Resolve Shot Match**

1. Set the grade of the first approved wide shot of a location as the "reference clip"
2. In the Color page, right-click any other clip → "Shot Match" → select the reference
3. Apply Shot Match, then adjust manually for what the algorithm got wrong

**For larger batches: Colourlab AI**

Batch-matches multiple clips against one graded "fingerprint" clip. Saves time when a scene has 8+ clips with varied lighting.

**Lock colour temperature in prompts.** The fastest version of colour matching is generating clips with the same colour temperature to begin with. Describe the light in Kelvin or with a specific adjective that includes colour: "warm tungsten 2900K interior" rather than "warm." Consistent descriptors narrow the variance each clip generates with.

---

## Speed ramping and motion blur

AI clips frequently generate without the motion blur that would exist in real footage at equivalent motion speeds. Fast movement reads as slightly plastic.

**Boris FX Continuum BCC+ Motion Blur ML** adds synthetic motion blur to clips that generated without it. Apply to clips with fast movement, not to wide slow clips where the effect is unnecessary.

**Optical-flow speed ramping** (DaVinci Resolve Neural Engine, Premiere Pro) is useful for extending or slowing a clip by generating interpolated frames. Works better on clips with slow, smooth motion; breaks down on fast motion or fine detail (hair, cloth in wind).

---

## NLE choice (working practice as of mid-2026)

**Premiere Pro 26.0:** AI-assisted editing — Firefly Boards for shot planning, Media Intelligence search across footage, Generative Extend for extending a clip up to 10 seconds with matched grain/lighting/camera motion (ambient audio only, no dialogue). First-pass assembly, ideation, extension.

**DaVinci Resolve Studio 20:** colour finishing, Dialogue Matcher for audio normalization across clips, high-quality speed ramping. Final finishing.

**In-tool editors (Kling, Hedra Studio):** useful for first-pass stitching within the same model's output. Not for final delivery.

---

## Pacing reference

| Video type | Average shot duration | Cuts per minute |
|---|---|---|
| Slow drama / character study | 5–10 seconds | 6–12 |
| Standard dialogue scene | 3–6 seconds | 10–20 |
| Action sequence | 1–3 seconds | 20–60 |
| Social media / reels | 1–2 seconds | 30–60 |

These are reference points, not rules. [PRACTITIONER: these are observed conventions from live-action editing, applied to AI clip assembly. Your scene may require very different pacing.] The right cut is the one that serves the emotion. A held frame of a character's face for eight seconds in the right context has more impact than twelve fast cuts.

The discipline for AI assembly: **plan the cut rate before generating clips.** If you are planning a 3-second average, prompt clips that are 4–5 seconds long (to allow trimming and head/tail removal). If you plan 8 seconds average, prompt 10-second clips.

---

## Checklist before delivery

- [ ] All clips trimmed (heads and tails)
- [ ] Colour matched to reference clip
- [ ] Screen direction consistent throughout
- [ ] Eyeline logic holds — each character looks toward where the other character is
- [ ] J/L-cuts applied at scene transitions and across key dialogue moments
- [ ] Sound design or score present — no clip left with only generator audio unless intentional
- [ ] First and last frames of the assembled sequence are both deliberate and clean
- [ ] Speed ramps (if any) tested on playback device, not just timeline preview
